# Cytotoxic CD4+ T cells are induced during infection with Chlamydia trachomatis

**Authors:** Joanna Olivas; Caterina Nogueira; Jennifer Helble; Michael N. Starnbach

**Affiliations:** *Department of Microbiology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA.

## Abstract

Chlamydia trachomatis (C. trachomatis) is the most common cause of bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) in both men and women. Immunity to C. trachomatis involves many cell types, but CD4+ T cells play a key role in protecting the host during natural infection. Specifically, IFNγ production by CD4+ T cells is the main effector responsible for bacterial clearance, yet the exact mechanism by which IFNγ confers protection is poorly defined. In our efforts to define the specific mechanisms for bacterial clearance, we now show that IFNγ upregulates expression of Major Histocompatibility Complex Class II (MHCII) on non-hematopoietic cells during C. trachomatis infection in vivo. We also find that MCHII expression on epithelial cells of the upper genital tract contributes to the efficient clearance of bacteria mediated by pathogen-specific CD4+ Th1 cells. As we further cataloged the protective mechanisms of C. trachomatis-specific CD4+ T cells, we found that the T cells also express granzyme B (GzmB) when co-incubated with infected cells. Additionally, during C. trachomatis infection of mice, primed activated-naïve CD4+ Th1 cells displayed elevated granzyme transcripts (GzmA, GzmB, GzmM, GzmK, GzmC) compared to memory CD4+ T cells in vivo. Finally, using intracellular cytokine staining and a GzmB−/− mouse strain, we show that C. trachomatis-specific CD4+ Th1 cells express granzyme B upon antigen stimulation and that this correlates with Chlamydia clearance in vivo. Together these results have led us to conclude that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells develop cytotoxic capacity through engagement with non-hematopoietic MHCII and this correlates to C. trachomatis clearance.

## INTRODUCTION

The obligate intracellular pathogen C. trachomatis is the most commonly reported sexually transmitted infection in the United States, with young women having particularly high rates [1–3]. Although treatable with antibiotics, C. trachomatis infection can be asymptomatic, and therefore many individuals are at high risk of being left untreated [1, 4, 5]. Moreover, patients remain susceptible to infection after treatment, suggesting a lack of natural protective immunity following infection. Repeated infection can lead to excessive inflammation of the upper genital tract, which may result in the development of severe disease outcomes such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy, and infertility [6–8]. Despite these adverse health outcomes, high rates of infection, and our poor ability to detect disease in the community, a vaccine to prevent the spread of infection and sequelae is not available [9].

To generate protection against future infections, vaccines aim to engage the adaptive immune system as this is crucial for immune memory formation. As such, mouse models of infection with C. trachomatis have been key to understanding the development of adaptive immunity against this pathogen since protective responses can be observed in previously-infected animals. In these studies, it has become clear that a CD4+ T cell response is central to protection against Chlamydia infection [10–12]. Moreover, mouse models also give us the ability to track Chlamydia-specific T cell responses by monitoring T cell receptor transgenic (TCRtg) T cells that have been introduced into the mouse prior to infection. In this study, we use NR1 TCRtg T cells, specific for the C. trachomatis protein Cta1 [13]. NR1 cells have been found to be protective in mice when these CD4+ T cells are skewed to a Th1 phenotype, which are typically characterized by the production of IFNγ [14]. Indeed, our group and others have shown that IFNγ is essential for host clearance of Chlamydia [15, 16]. However, it has not been clear how IFNγ-producing CD4+ Th1 cells clear bacteria from infected epithelial cells, which typically do not constitutively express MHC class II (MHCII).

In epithelial cells, immune surveillance usually occurs through the recognition of pathogen-derived antigens presented in the context of MHC class I molecules to CD8+ T cells [17]. This recognition can result in the release of cytotoxic molecules by CD8+ T cells to kill infected target cells. However, during Chlamydia infection, CD8+ T cells have been shown to be dispensable for bacterial clearance, as these cells are inhibited by the immunoinhibitory molecule PD-L1 (programmed death-ligand 1) upregulated on uterine epithelial cells during C. trachomatis infection. PD-L1 engagement results in decreased numbers of IFNγ-producing CD8+ T cells, which are sufficient but not necessary to clear C. trachomatis infection [18–20]. Thus, in the absence of a strong CD8+ T cell response, CD4+ Th1 cells have proven to be integral to protection against Chlamydia infection,

Classically, CD4+ T cells have been thought to act primarily as helpers through the secretion of cytokines [17]. Hence, it is well established that clearance of C. trachomatis is mediated by the production of IFNγ by CD4+ Th1 cells, yet the ultimate mechanism by which they protect has been poorly understood. Moreover, it is now evident that CD4+ T cells can also develop cytotoxic responses reminiscent of those of CD8+ T cells and play a role in fighting chronic conditions and viral infections. However, there are few studies on the cytotoxic CD4+ T cell (CD4+CTL) response to intracellular pathogens [21–24]. In particular, the CD4+CTL response to C. trachomatis has never been explored in vivo.

Here we showed that CD4+ T lymphocytes with a CTL phenotype are present in the spleen of mice infected with C. trachomatis. These cells display in vitro and in vivo cytotoxicity which correlates to lower bacterial burden in vivo. Moreover, we find that host expression of MHCII is essential for the production of GzmB by CD4+ CTL cells and that expression of MHCII molecules on epithelial cells, dependent on IFNγ sensing, is required for C. trachomatis clearance in a murine model.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Growth and isolation of bacteria.

Chlamydia trachomatis serovar L2 (434/Bu; ATCC) was propagated in McCoy cells as described previously [25, 26]. Aliquots of purified elementary bodies were stored at −80°C in SPG buffer (250mM sucrose, 10 mM sodium phosphate, 5 mM L-glutamic acid) and thawed immediately prior use.

### Mice.

Six-to-8-week-old C57BL/6J mice, B6.129S2-H2dlAb1-Ea/J, B6.129S7-Ifngr1tm1Agt/J, B6.SJL-PtprcaPepb/BoyJ were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME). NR1 mice that recognize a peptide from the C. trachomatis antigen Cta1 (residues 133 to 152) have been previously described [13]. To generate GzmB−/− NR1 mice, GzmB−/− mice were crossed with NR1 mice. GzmB−/− and NR1+ status was determined using PCR. All mice were housed in the Harvard Medical School Center for Animal Resources and Comparative Medicine, and all experiments were approved by Harvard’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

### Cell culture.

Murine embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells were isolated from embryonic day 12.5–14.5 embryos. Cells were then cultured and grown with DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 5 mM Sodium pyruvate and HEPES. C57BL/6 mouse primary uterine epithelial cells were purchased from Cell Biologics (Chicago, IL) and cultured according to manufacturer’s instructions.

### Expression of MHCII assays.

For expression of MHCII, 200,000 MEF cells were seeded into a 6-well plate and pre-treated with recombinant mouse IFNγ (Recombinant Murine IFN-γ; Peprotech, Rocky Hill, NJ) for a period of 24 h. Cells were then detached using PBS with 5 mM EDTA and incubated at 37°C for 10 m. Cells were then stained with Zombie NIR™ Fixable Viability Kit to test for cell viability, and I-Ab (clone AF6–120.1) to examine MHCII expression, using a BD LSRII flow cytometer ( Franklin Lakes, New Jersey, U.S.)

### Bone marrow preparation and bone marrow chimeric mice.

To isolate hematopoietic cells in adult mice, tibias, femurs, and pelvic bones were removed, and bone marrow (BM) was released by crushing in ice-cold PBS, followed by passage through 70 μm filters. Cells were then resuspended in tris-buffered ammonium chloride lysis buffer (17 mM Tris-HCL-pH 7.5, 150 mM NH4CL) for 3–5 minutes, followed by washing and suspension in PBS. To make the bone marrow chimeric mice, host mice were lethally irradiated at 600 rad twice with a 4 h interim. Host mice were injected i.v. with 7 × 106 bone marrow cells from donor mice post-second irradiation. The recipient mice were given drinking water containing antibiotics (200 mg Sulfamethozazole, 40 mg Trimethoprim, 0.5% Alcohol) for 2 weeks after irradiation.

### Peripheral blood (PB) analysis.

Transplant recipients were assessed for donor cell contribution to the PB. Blood was collected from the tail into heparinized capillary tubes, followed by lysis in red blood cell lysis buffer. Cells were then resuspended in PBS/2% FBS and analyzed for donor contribution using a LSR II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences). For blood analysis, cells were stained with anti-mouse CD45.1 (clone A20) and CD45.2 (clone 104) antibodies.

### T cell adoptive transfers and Th1 Skewing.

CD4+ T cells were isolated and purified from secondary lymphoid organs from NR1 mice using a Dynabeads untouched mouse CD4 cell kit (Invitrogen). T cells were stimulated using irradiated splenocytes from a C57BL/6 mouse that had been pulsed with 5 μM of Cta1 peptide (Cta1133–152) at a 4:1 simulator/T cell ratio. Cells were cultured for 5 days in RPMI 1640 (Invitrogen) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, L-glutamine, HEPES, 50 mM 2-mercaptoethanol, 50 U/ml penicillin and 50 mg/ml streptomycin along with 10 ng/ml interleukin-12 (Peprotech, Rocky Hill, NJ) and 10 μg/ml anti-IL-4 (Bio X Cell, West Lebanon, NH). A total of 106 Th1-skewed NR1 T cells were injected i.v. in a 200-μl volume into recipient mice 1 day prior to infection with C. trachomatis.

### Infection of mice and preparation of tissue.

One week prior to transcervical infection, mice were treated subcutaneously with 2.5 mg of medroxyprogesterone. For i.v. infections, mice did not receive medroxyprogesterone. Mice were infected transcervically with 5 × 106 inclusion-forming units (IFUs) of C. trachomatis in 10 μl of SPG buffer using a Non-Surgical Embryo Transfer (NSET) device (ParaTechs, Lexington, KY) as describe previously [12]. Uninfected control mice were inoculated in the same manner with 10 ul of SPG buffer alone. At specific timepoints post-infection, upper genital tracts (uterine horns and ovaries) and draining lymph nodes were harvested. Upper genital tracts were minced with scalpels, incubated in Hanks balanced salt solution (HBSS)/ Ca2+/ Mg2+ containing 1 mg/ml of type XI collagenase and 50 Kunitz units/ml of DNase for 30 min at 37°C and then washed in Ca2+ /Mg2+ -free PBS containing 5 mM EDTA. Tissues were then ground between frosted microscope slides prior to filtration through 70-μm-pore-size mesh. Following i.v. infection, single-cell suspensions of lymph nodes and spleen were prepared by grinding the tissue between frosted microscope slides.

### Cytotoxicity Assays.

LDH released in the medium was measured using an LDH assay kit-WST (Dojindo, Rockville, MD) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, C57BL/6 mouse primary uterine epithelial cells, purchased from CellBiologics (Chicago, IL), were co-incubated with Th1 skewed antigen specific CD4+ T cells at various T cell concentrations in a 96-well plate. After 48 h of co-incubation, supernatant from each well was transferred into a new 96-well plate for the LDH assay and mixed with 100 μl of reagent. The samples were then incubated at room temperature for 30 m, protected from light. Stop solution was added to each well and the optical density at 490 nm was measured using a Synergy MX Biotek microplate reader (Agilent, Santa Clara CA).

### Flow cytometry.

All antibodies were purchased from BioLegend except where otherwise noted. Following isolation, cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies against mouse TCRVα (clone B20.1), TCRβ 8.3 (clone 1B3.3; BD Biosciences), CD4 (clone RM4–5), CD8 (clone 53–6.7), I-Ab (clone AF6–120.1), and CD326+ (clone G8.8). To assess cell viability a LIVE/DEAD Fixable Aqua Dead cell stain kit was used (Invitrogen). To assess granzyme B expression, cells were fixed and permeabilized using a fixation/permeabilization kit (Invitrogen) and then stained with an anti-granzyme B antibody (clone GB11). AccuCheck counting beads (Invitrogen) were used to determine absolute cell counts. Data were collected on an LSR II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and were analyzed using Flowjo (Tree Star, Ashland, OR).

### In vitro cell proliferation staining.

In vitro skewed NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells and GzmB−/− NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells were washed twice with PBS. Then, cells were suspended in PBS at a concentration of 10 × 106 cells/ml and labeled with 10μM of cell proliferation 450 dye (eBioscience) at 37°C for 20 min. Cells were mixed every 10 m to provide uniform staining. Cells were then resuspended into a 50:50 mixture of T cell media (10% fetal bovine serum, L-glutamine, HEPES, 50 mM 2-mercaptoethanol, 50 U/ml penicillin and 50 mg/ml streptomycin) and complete fetal bovine serum and incubated for 5 m in ice to stop labelling. Subsequently, cells were washed 4 times with T cell media and finally resuspended in PBS. These cells were then analyzed in a LSR II flow cytometer prior to transfer into experimental mice at a concentration of 1 × 106 cells in 200μl.

### RNA sequencing and transcriptome analysis.

RNA sequencing was conducted as previously described [27] and re-analyzed for the purposes of this study. Briefly, iliac lymph nodes from six individual mice were pooled per biological replicate. RNA sequencing was conducted on biological triplicates of equal numbers (no more than 103 cells) of double-sorted memory and naïve NR1 T cells. The sequencing data are available in the Gene Expression Omnibus under data repository accession number GSE146265. RNA sequencing data were read into R (v.4.1.1) and the DESeq2 package (v1.38.2) [28] was used to identify differential gene expression. The pheatmap package (v.1.0.12) and ggplot2 (v.3.4.0) were used to plot the heatmap and volcano plot, respectively.

### Quantitative PCR.

Bacterial burden was determined using quantitative PCR as previously described [29]. Briefly, DNA was extracted from genital tract or spleen tissue using a QIAmp DNA minikit (Qiagen). Chlamydia 16S DNA (forward primer, 5’- GGAGGCTGCAGTCGAGAATCT-3’; reverse primer, 5’- TTACAACCCTAGAGCCTTCATCACA-3’) and mouse GAPHD (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) were quantified using primer pairs and dually labeled probes (IDT, San Jose, CA, or Applied Biosciences).

### Statistical analysis.

Statistical analysis was performed using Prism software (GraphPad). Volcano plot enrichment P values were determined using χ2 test in Microsoft Excel. Statistical analysis for flow cytometry data was performed using Prism (GraphPad). Differences were considered statistically significant if the P value was less than 0.05. *P ≤ 0.05, **P < 0.01, *** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001. All data are represented as means ± standard error of the mean (SEM).

## RESULTS

### Sensing of IFNγ by non-hematopoietic cells is necessary for CD4+ Th1-mediated clearance of C. trachomatis and induces expression of MHCII molecules in uterine epithelial cells.

T cell-mediated clearance of Chlamydia infection relies on CD4+ Th1 cells, which produce IFNγ, as well as the ability of host cells to sense IFNγ [14, 15]. However, it is unclear which host cells are required to sense IFNγ in order to protect against this pathogen. Therefore, we created two distinct bone marrow chimera mice to test which host cell compartment requires IFNγ sensing for CD4+ Th1 cell-mediated clearance. In the first set of mice, wild-type (WT) mice were irradiated and then reconstituted with bone marrow obtained from IFNγ receptor knockout mice (IFNγR−/−), generating mice in which only the non-hematopoietic cells, but not hematopoietic cells can sense and respond to IFNγ. In the second set, irradiated IFNγR−/− mice were reconstituted with bone marrow from WT mice, generating mice in which only hematopoietic cells, but not the non-hematopoietic cells, can sense and respond to IFNγ. We then transferred polarized NR1 C. trachomatis-specific Th1 cells into both groups of mice. One day after transfer, mice were inoculated transcervically with C. trachomatis, and bacterial burden was assessed by qPCR five days later (Figure 1A).

As in our previous studies, we observed that WT mice that received adoptive transfer of protective NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells had lower bacterial burden when compared to WT mice that did not receive these protective cells [12, 14, 15]. Similar to WT mice, the chimeric mice which can sense IFNγ in their non-hematopoietic cells, such as epithelial cells, had a lower bacterial burden in the presence of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells. In contrast, we observed exacerbated bacterial burden in the uterus of chimeric mice in which only the hematopoietic cells, such as antigen-presenting cells (APCs), can sense IFNγ. These findings show that protection conferred by the NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells requires the ability of host non-hematopoietic cells to sense IFNγ (Figure 1B).

IFNγ is a potent immunoregulatory molecule known to coordinate a diverse array of cellular programs [30]. Importantly, we have now shown that the host non-hematopoietic compartment requires sensing of IFNγ to combat Chlamydia infection (Figure 1B). The involvement of CD4+ T cells, non-hematopoietic cells, and IFNγ suggest that a complex cellular process may be involved, such as IFNγ-mediated expression of Major Histocompatibility Complex II (MHCII). Traditionally, MHCII molecules are primarily expressed on professional APCs, where peptide-MHCII complexes activate CD4+ T cells. However, it is increasingly appreciated that non-hematopoietic cells can also upregulate MHCII molecules when stimulated by IFNγ [21, 31–33]. Indeed, using flow cytometry, we found that in the presence of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells, the chimeric mice capable of sensing IFNγ through the non-hematopoietic compartment had higher surface expression of MHCII molecules on epithelial cells (CD326+ cells) than when the IFNγ-producing T cells were not present. However, we did not see enhanced levels of MHCII expression on epithelial cells from chimeric mice given NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells that only sense IFNγ in their hematopoietic compartment or in WT mice that did not receive the NR1 T cells (Figure 1C). Together, these results suggest that non-hematopoietic cells mediate IFNγ-dependent bacterial clearance and that induction of MHCII expression may contribute to this phenotype.

### Expression of MHCII molecules in uterine non-hematopoietic cells is necessary for Chlamydia- specific CD4+ Th1-mediated protection against C. trachomatis.

To test if the expression of MHCII molecules in uterine epithelial cells influences the course of C. trachomatis infection, we generated chimeric mice that are deficient in the ability to express MHCII molecules in their non-hematopoietic compartment but do express MHCII in hematopoietic cells such as APCs. To do this, MHCII knockout (MHCII−/−) mice were irradiated and reconstituted with WT bone marrow. As a control, WT mice were irradiated and transplanted with WT bone marrow, resulting in mice that express MHCII molecules in all cells. At week 6 post-procedure, Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells were transferred into the mice, followed by transcervical inoculation with C. trachomatis 24hr later. Five days post-inoculation, the upper genital tract was harvested and C. trachomatis burden was assessed by qPCR (Figure 2A).

First, we showed that WT mice have lower Chlamydia burden when they receive a transfer of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells, relative to WT mice that did not receive T cells. Chimeric mice into which protective T cells were transferred, but where non-hematopoietic lack MHCII expression showed higher burdens, similar to WT mice that did not receive protective T cells (Figure 2B). These observations led us to conclude that MHCII expression in non-hematopoietic cells is required for Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cell-mediated protection against C. trachomatis.

### Primed naïve Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells upregulate cytolytic molecules during C. trachomatis infection

When naïve CD4+ T cells recognize antigen-MHCII complexes they proliferate and differentiate into various specialized subsets with the capacity to produce specific cytokines and through them promote various immune responses [17]. Therefore, cytokine production has been the central focus of CD4+ T cell immunity. Yet, a growing body of evidence has shown that CD4+ T cells also have effector functions beyond cytokine expression and can cause direct cytolysis of target cells, an activity formerly attributed mostly to CD8+ T cells [21, 22, 34]. Evidence that direct cytolysis might be a CD4+ T cell effector role during C. trachomatis infection was found in data from a previous study we conducted. Helble et al. [27] sought to compare the difference in the development of memory and primed naïve T cells during C. trachomatis infection. In brief, naïve B6 mice (CD90.2+/+) received CD90.1+/− NR1 intravenously, followed by a transcervical infection of 5×106 IFU of C. trachomatis the following day. Infected mice were allowed to clear the infection and establish a memory population (CD90.1+/− T cells). These mice then received CD90.1+/+ T cells and were reinfected with C. trachomatis one day later. Five days post-secondary infection, memory (CD90.1+/−), and primed naïve (CD90.1+/+) T cells were double sorted and subjected to bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) [27]. By further examining the dataset now, we find that encounter with antigen by primed naïve (CD90.1+/+) NR1 CD4+ T cells, which we previously established were more Th1 like compared to memory NR1 T cells, drives upregulation of granzyme transcripts (GzmA, GzmB, GzmM, GzmK, GzmC) compared to that observed in Chlamydia-specific memory (CD90.1+/−) CD4+ T cells. In particular, we observed that among the cytolytic molecules, GzmB was the most significantly upregulated in primed naïve NR1 CD4+ T cells (Figure 3 A and B). In summary, these data suggest that NR1 CD4+ Th1s may have cytolytic potential during C. trachomatis infection through the upregulation of cytotoxic molecules like GzmB.

### Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells show expression of Granzyme B and can kill Chlamydia-infected cells in vitro

As we continued to investigate the ability of NR1 CD4+ Th1 lymphocytes to acquire cytolytic functions during C. trachomatis infection, we developed a cell co-culture approach using a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cell line as an in vitro model. Since MCHII expression is critical for presentation to CD4+ T cells, we assessed the ability of MEF cells to express MHCII molecules after stimulation with various concentrations of recombinant murine IFNγ (U/ml). One day post stimulation, MHCII expression on the MEFs was analyzed by flow cytometry. MEFs treated with recombinant murine IFNγ showed increased MCHII expression compared to untreated cells, and the increase in MHCII expression appeared to be dose-dependent. Importantly, we did not observe a significant change in the expression of MHCII molecules upon infection of these cells with C. trachomatis, indicating that expression of MHCII on MEF cells is dependent on sensing of IFNγ and is unaffected by C. trachomatis infection. These results are concordant with our in vivo observations above, showing that IFNγ sensing can drive expression of MHCII in non-hematopoietic cells during Chlamydia infection (Figures 4A and 4B).

Next, we tested the ability of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells to express granzyme B when co-incubated with infected vs. uninfected MEFs and found that the T cells showed higher production of GzmB when the MEFs were infected. As expected, we observed an increase GzmB expression by CD4+ Th1 cells only when they were co-incubated with infected cells (Figure 4C and 4D).

Granzyme B is a serine protease released by cytotoxic lymphocytes and mediates cellular apoptosis in addition to its protease activity [35].To confirm whether GzmB also induces cell death, we measured Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) levels in the supernatant of primary WT uterine epithelial cells, obtained from Cell Biologics, co-cultured with Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells. After 2 days of co-incubation, there were greater levels of LDH release from infected epithelial cells (MOI of 1) co-incubated with NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells relative to uninfected epithelial cells co-incubated with the T cells. Furthermore, we observed a corresponding increase in LDH release from infected epithelial cells as more T cells were added to the culture. Infection alone was not sufficient to induce epithelial cell death as measured by lower LDH release when T cells were not present with the infected cells. We did not observe LDH release from infected NR1 T cells alone or epithelial cells cultured alone (Figure 4E). Together, these results indicate that GzmB expressing NR1s can kill C. trachomatis infected epithelial cells in a dose-dependent manner.

### NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells express Granzyme B in vivo and correlate with lower bacterial burden during C. trachomatis infection.

In the experiments above, we observed the functional capacity of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells to express GzmB and display cytotoxicity in vitro. Additionally, we showed the importance of MHCII expression for bacterial clearance in vivo (Figure 2B). To connect these observations, we tested whether NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells can express GzmB in vivo and whether it requires MHCII expression. Previous studies examining cytotoxic CD4+ T cells in various biological contexts have indicated that these cells typically represent a small minority within the overall CD4+ T cell population. Therefore, we decided to transition to a systemic infection model. This allowed for a more efficient exploration of granzyme B expression in Chlamydia-specific CD4+ T cells in vivo, as it enhances the likelihood of Chlamydia-specific CD4+ T cells encountering Chlamydia antigen. Thus, for this experiment, we labeled NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells with Cell Proliferation Dye (CPD) eFlour 450 and transferred 106 of these T cells per mouse into groups of WT and MHCII−/− mice. One day after T cell transfer, mice were challenged intravenously with 107 IFU of C. trachomatis. Mouse spleens were harvested 4 days after infection to assess GzmB expression in NR1 CD4+ Th1 as well as bacterial burden. For controls, we also transferred NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells into uninfected mice and additionally included WT mice and MHCII−/− mice that did not receive any transferred cells.

As anticipated, our findings show that proliferation of Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells occurs exclusively in the presence of Chlamydia antigen, as evidenced by a downward shift in the fluorescence intensity of CPD eFlour 450 towards zero. In line with our prior in vitro observations, we noted that only in infected wild-type mice did live Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells (Supplemental Figure 1) demonstrate the capacity to express GzmB. Conversely, we did not observe depletion of CPD eFlour 450 or expression of GzmB in Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells transferred into uninfected wild-type or MHCII−/− mice (Figure 5A and 5B). NR1 CD4+ Th1 GzmB+ cells represent around 10–20% of the CD4+ T cells in the spleen of infected WT mice. Importantly, we did not observe expression of GzmB in our MHCII−/− groups regardless of infection, indicating that MHCII-dependent antigen recognition is necessary for the expression of GzmB by NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 5C). This difference in GzmB expression was not due to a difference in the numbers of total CD4+ T cells, or migration of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells, as the various groups did not display significantly different percentages or absolute numbers of these cells in the spleen (Figure 5D). Of note, we do expect a difference in the overall levels of CD4+ T cells between WT and MHCII−/− mice, as the latter mice show a decrease in mature CD4+ T cells due to a lack of MHCII expression in the thymus. This, however, did not inhibit the ability of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells to migrate into the spleen, as the majority of CD4+ T cells found in the spleen of MHCII−/− mice were NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells, illustrated by the higher percentage of CD4+ Va+ CD90.1+ T cells present (Figure 5E). Together, these results indicate that NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells are capable of expressing GzmB upon Chlamydia antigen stimulation in vivo.

Given that our previous experiments showed that NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells are important for bacterial clearance, we then wondered if production of GzmB also correlated with decreased bacterial burden. Thus, we examined bacterial burden in the spleen of the experimental groups above using qPCR. Consistent with our previous experiments, we observed that WT mice that received adoptive transfer of NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells, which are GzmB+, had lower bacterial burden compared to mice that did not receive these GzmB-producing CD4+ T cells. Conversely, we observed higher levels of bacterial burden in the MHCII−/− mice groups independently of whether they received NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells or not (Figure 5F). Together, these results show that NR1 CD4+ Th1 cells are capable of expressing GzmB upon Chlamydia antigen stimulation and that the production of GzmB correlates with protection against C. trachomatis in vivo.

### Granzyme B expression by Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells is contingent upon antigen presentation via MHCII and may play a role in protection against C. trachomatis infection

Our previous in vivo experiments demonstrated that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells are capable of expressing GzmB in vivo, and that this correlates with decreased bacterial burden in C. trachomatis-infected mice. To confirm whether GzmB expression directly influences bacterial clearance, we generated GzmB knockout NR1 transgenic mice (GzmB−/− NR1 mice). GzmB−/− Chlamydia-specific CD4+ and WT Chlamydia-specific CD4+ T cells were skewed to a Th1 phenotype as previously described. Following Th1 induction, both cell types were labeled with CPD eFluor 450. Immediately, Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells (Thy 1.1+) were transferred into B6 mice (Thy1.2+), while GzmB−/− Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 (CD45.2+) were transferred into Pep Boy mice (CD45.1+). These different congenic markers allowed for the tracking of Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells accurately in each recipient mouse. Twenty-four hours post-transfer, mice were challenged with C. trachomatis. Spleens were harvested 4 days later to assess GzmB expression via flow cytometry and bacterial burden by qPCR. Control groups included both GzmB-competent and GzmB-deficient Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells transferred into uninfected mice, as well as WT and MHCII−/− mice without transferred cells.

Consistent with our previous findings, we observed that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells are capable of expressing GzmB in the presence of Chlamydia antigen, as indicated by a rightward shift in GzmB fluorescence intensity in infected WT mice. In contrast, GzmB−/− Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells failed to express GzmB even when Pep Boy mice, which differ from WT mice only in their CD45+ congenic marker, were infected with C. trachomatis. Uniformly, no GzmB expression was detected in either Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells or GzmB−/− Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells transferred into uninfected or infected MCHII−/− mice (Figure 6A). This shows that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells obtained from our GzmB−/− NR1 mice are indeed deficient in their ability to produce GzmB. Importantly, GzmB-competent and GzmB-deficient Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells exhibited proliferation upon C. trachomatis infection (Figure 6A). This is demonstrated by the depletion of CPD eFlour 450 in both cell types, indicating that knockout of GzmB did not impede the capacity of Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells to recognize C. trachomatis antigen and undergo activation.

Upon examining bacterial burden, although the observed trend was not statistically significant, it remained consistent with our previous observations. Specifically, WT mice that received adoptive transfer of Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells exhibited a decrease in bacterial burden compared to WT mice that did not undergo adoptive transfer (P-value= 0.063). Conversely, when PepBoy mice received GzmB−/− Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells, the observed reduction in bacterial burden was not as pronounced (P-value= 0.621). Additionally, we did not observe enhanced C. trachomatis clearance in infected MHCII−/− mice following the transfer of either GzmB-competent or GzmB-deficient Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 6B). While these findings might appear somewhat disheartening, the absence of a conclusive determination regarding the protective efficacy of cytotoxic Chlamydia-CD4+ Th1 cells stems from the lack of a significant distinction between our B6 + NR1 and B6 control groups. This discrepancy could be attributed to the inherent variability in mouse experiments, yet our findings still hint at a possible involvement of cytotoxic CD4+ Th1 cells in protection against C. trachomatis. Importantly, these experiments demonstrate that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ T cells can become cytotoxic in vivo and that this is dependent on antigen presentation via MHCII.

## DISCUSSION

Immunity to C. trachomatis requires IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells to control infection [14–16, 36–38]. However, the mechanisms by which CD4+ Th1 cells and the IFNγ produced by them lead to the clearance of C. trachomatis infection was incompletely known. In this study, we sought to gain deeper insight into bacterial clearance by CD4+ T cells. Our study demonstrates that CD4+ T cell recognition of Chlamydia antigen presented by MHCII on non-hematopoietic cells in vivo results in bacterial clearance through cytotoxic activity.

IFNγ, a critical cytokine for controlling Chlamydia infection, has been shown to limit bacterial proliferation through various activities. For instance, IFNγ can mediate protection by enhancing phagocytosis by macrophages and increasing the expression of MHCII [39] on professional APCs. Moreover, IFNγ can inhibit Chlamydia growth by inducing antimicrobial defenses in infected cells, such as the expression of the metabolic enzyme indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), which deprives C. trachomatis of intracellular pools of the essential amino acid, tryptophan [40–43]. Another mechanism is intracellular killing via the induction of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), which catalyzes the production of antimicrobial nitrogen species [23, 44, 45]. The relative contributions of these mechanisms depend on the host cell type and Chlamydia spp. tropism, making it hard to attribute clearance to a single IFNγ-dependent activity. Overall, it seems likely that protection against C. trachomatis requires multiple IFNγ-dependent pathways, including some that have remained undescribed.

As we sought to uncover additional IFNγ-dependent mechanisms by which CD4+ Th1 cells might limit C. trachomatis growth, we focused on determining which cell types could be responding to this cytokine. Bone marrow chimeric mice allowed us to separate the biological effects of IFNγ on the hematopoietic versus the stromal compartment, and using this tool, we showed that sensing of IFNγ through the non-hematopoietic compartment is required for optimal CD4+ Th1-mediated clearance of C. trachomatis (Figure 1B). Since effective T cell function requires TCR-MHCII interaction, we wondered if non-hematopoietic cells could express MHCII during infection. It has been established that IFNγ can activate the Class II transactivator type IV promoter (CIITA pIV), known to regulate the expression of MHCII in non-hematopoietic cells [11]. Indeed, we found that in response to IFNγ there was increased expression of MHCII complexes on the cell surface of these cells, and this increase was neither induced by nor affected by C. trachomatis infection (Figures 1B and 4C). These observations are in alignment with previous in vitro studies, where treatment of C. muridarum-infected epithelial cells with recombinant IFNγ led to the expression of MHCII [24]. Our data confirm and expand these findings by showing that the IFNγ produced by CD4+ Th1 cells in vivo is sufficient to upregulate MHCII expression in non-hematopoietic cells. Importantly, these data support a model where non-hematopoietic cells participate in adaptive immune responses to C. trachomatis, an organism that primarily infects and develops within these cells.

Recent studies in non-hematopoietic cells have led to a deeper understanding of how their expression of MHCII functions to modulate immune responses at mucosal surfaces [32, 33, 46–51]. For instance, Shenoy et al. showed that lung epithelial cells function as antigen-presenting cells and help shape the CD4+ T cell response during S. pneumoniae infection [52]. Here, we show similar observations in the context of C. trachomatis infection, where IFNγ-induced MHCII complexes in non-hematopoietic cells are necessary for driving a protective Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 response against this pathogen (Figure 2). This also suggested that there should be a direct interaction between C. trachomatis-infected cells and Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells required for optimal clearance of C. trachomatis in vivo.

Generally, CD4+ T cells regulate immune responses through the secretion of various cytokines upon antigen recognition. Nonetheless, CD4+ T cells with cytotoxic features (CD4+ CTLs) have been increasingly reported in humans and mice [21, 34, 53–60]. These cells are characterized by the secretion of cytotoxic molecules, such as GzmB, and their ability to kill target cells in an MHCII-restricted manner [22]. In earlier studies, Jayarapu et al. hinted at the direct interaction between CD4+ T cells and C. muridarum-infected epithelial cells in vitro. This study found that CD4+ T cell degranulation and perforin secretion could occur in response to C. muridarum-infected cells. Moreover, they also noted that perforin might be found to play a complex role in C. muridarum clearance in vivo [23, 61].

Based on our data above showing that deletion of MHCII in non-hematopoietic cells results in higher bacterial burden in mice and previous reports suggesting that CD4+ T cell may acquire cytotoxicity abilities, we asked whether MHCII on non-hematopoietic cells instructs CD4+ T cells to display cytotoxic effector functions in vivo. Indeed, we find that activated-naive CD4+ T cells, which become Th1-like, develop cytotoxic abilities as they upregulate Granzyme transcripts. This demonstrates that inflammatory conditions under C. trachomatis infection provide the right environment for antigen-experienced CD4+ T cells to differentiate further into cytotoxic cells (Figure 3). Moreover, we show that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 (Supplemental Figure 1) can produce functional GzmB when presented with Chlamydia antigen both in vitro and in vivo (Figures 4 and 5). During C. trachomatis infection, about 10–20% of the total population of transferred Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells express GzmB in vivo (Figures 4 and 5). Such a low population is not surprising, given that cytotoxic CD4+ T cells typically represent a small percentage of the total CD4+ T cells seen during infection with other pathogens [21, 22]. Moreover, we show that the production of GzmB by these cells correlates with lowering bacterial burden in the spleen of Chlamydia-infected mice (Figure 5F and Figure 6). Together, our observations indicate that Chlamydia-specific CD4+ Th1 cells may play a direct role in the killing of C. trachomatis-infected cells through the secretion of cytotoxic molecules in vivo. Future investigation will be required to conclusively determine the impact of GzmB expression by CD4 T cells in C. trachomatis infection.

IFNγ coordinates a vast array of cellular programs in immunocytes and target tissue [30]. In our system, we observed that the deletion of the IFNγR in non-hematopoietic cells highly impacted the ability of mice to reduce bacterial load. Similarly, deleting MHCII complexes in these cells also prevented mice from clearing bacteria. Nevertheless, the effects of MHCII deletion were not as robust as when we deleted IFNγR in non-hematopoietic cells. These observations are not surprising given that IFNγ has multiple effects to lessen bacterial burden. Thus, MHCII expression on non-hematopoietic cells plays a role in C. trachomatis clearance in conjunction with other IFNγ- dependent mechanisms.

Altogether, our work uncovers a novel role for IFNγ-induced expression of MHCII in non-hematopoietic cells in supporting C. trachomatis clearance and the engagement of cytotoxic CD4+ T cells. Significantly, our study provides further supporting evidence for the development of a vaccine that stimulates a robust CD4+ T cell response, in part because such a response might promote C. trachomatis clearance through direct means.
